learn.title: Cash flow, forecasting and profit versus cash

sections.heading: Cash movement is not the same as profit
sections.body: Cash flow tracks money actually entering and leaving the bank. Profit is an accounting measure, so it can include credit sales before customers have paid and costs before or after cash is paid. A business can report a profit yet lack enough cash to pay wages, suppliers or loan instalments. Borrowing brings cash into the business, but it is not sales profit.

sections.heading: How a cash-flow forecast is built
sections.body: For each future period, start with the opening cash balance. Estimate cash receipts for that period, then estimate cash payments. Subtract payments from receipts to find net cash flow. Add net cash flow to the opening balance to obtain the closing balance. The closing balance normally becomes the next period's opening balance. Use expected payment dates, rather than the date a sale or expense is recorded.

sections.heading: The timing chain behind cash pressure
sections.body:
Credit sale → receivable → customer pays later → cash receipt.

Inventory purchase → cash payment now → inventory sold later → possible credit sale → cash receipt later.

Rapid growth → more inventory and more receivables → cash leaves before more customer cash arrives → greater financing need. This sequence explains why growth can create a shortage even where sales are rising.

sections.heading: Reading a simple forecast
sections.body: A retailer begins April with £20,000 cash. It expects receipts of £70,000 and payments of £82,000. First find net cash flow: £70,000 minus £82,000 is negative £12,000. Then add this to opening cash: £20,000 plus negative £12,000 gives a closing balance of £8,000. The business remains cash-positive, but has a smaller buffer against late-paying customers or unexpected costs.

sections.heading: Test the effect of delayed receipts
sections.body: Using the retailer forecast, suppose £20,000 of expected customer receipts will arrive next month instead. Receipts for April fall from £70,000 to £50,000. Net cash flow becomes £50,000 minus £82,000, or negative £32,000. Adding this to the £20,000 opening balance produces a negative £12,000 closing balance. The forecast has identified a financing need before the shortage happens.

sections.heading: Put entries in the forecast at the cash date
sections.body: Example: a £50,000 credit sale made in June is forecast as a July cash receipt if the customer is expected to pay in July. Non-example: entering that £50,000 as June cash received just because it is June revenue. Similarly, loan proceeds are a cash inflow but are not revenue or profit.

sections.heading: A forecast is conditional, not a promise
sections.body: A forecast does not tell managers exactly what will happen. It is based on assumptions about sales, customer payment dates, costs and finance. Late payment, a customer default or a changed lending decision can make the outcome different. Managers should examine scenarios, especially those involving delayed receipts and higher payments, rather than relying only on one predicted closing balance.

sections.heading: Choosing a cash-flow remedy involves trade-offs
sections.body: Possible actions include collecting receivables faster, negotiating longer supplier credit, reducing inventory, delaying investment, obtaining finance or changing payment arrangements. Each can have drawbacks. Tighter collection may upset customers; longer supplier terms may damage supplier relationships; lower inventory can cause stock shortages; delayed investment may restrict capacity and growth; additional finance raises risk or future payment commitments. Choose actions by considering timing, customer and supplier effects, growth needs and access to finance.

sections.heading: Explain the difference in your own words
sections.body: A wholesaler is profitable but is short of cash while sales are growing quickly. Explain the likely timing sequence involving inventory, credit customers and customer receipts. Then identify one action to improve cash flow and one possible disadvantage of that action.

key_terms.definition: Cash received by a business during a period.
Cash paid by a business during a period.
Cash inflows minus cash outflows for a period.
Cash available at the start of a period.
Cash available at the end of a period after net cash flow is added to the opening balance.
An estimate of future cash receipts, payments and balances.
Money owed to the business by a customer, often following a credit sale.
Money the business owes to a supplier or other creditor.

items.prompt: State the relationship between opening balance, net cash flow and closing balance in a cash-flow forecast.
items.answer: Closing balance equals opening balance plus net cash flow.
items.explanation: The opening cash is adjusted by the period's inflows and outflows, represented by net cash flow.

items.prompt: Construct the missing figures for May: opening balance £9,000; cash receipts £31,000; cash payments £35,000. Give net cash flow and closing balance.
items.explanation: Receipts minus payments are -£4,000. Adding this fall to the £9,000 opening balance leaves £5,000.

items.prompt: A business makes a £12,000 credit sale in August and expects payment in October. In which month should the £12,000 be entered as a cash receipt in the forecast?
items.explanation: The forecast records when cash is expected to be received, not when revenue is recognised from the credit sale.

items.prompt: A growing online retailer has cash tied up in slow-moving inventory. Suggest one suitable way to improve its cash flow.
items.answer: Reduce slow-moving inventory, for example by ordering less or selling excess stock.
items.explanation: This can release cash that would otherwise remain tied up in unsold goods.

items.prompt: A café plans to delay replacing an ageing coffee machine to preserve cash. Judge one benefit and one drawback of this decision.
items.answer: Benefit: cash is retained in the short term. Drawback: the old machine may reduce capacity or reliability, harming service and future sales.
items.explanation: Delaying investment can solve an immediate liquidity problem but may create operational and growth costs.

items.prompt: A manager says: 'We made a £40,000 credit sale this month, so our bank balance must have risen by £40,000.' Is this correct?
items.answer: No. The bank balance rises only when the customer pays.
items.explanation: A credit sale may increase revenue and profit, but it creates a receivable until cash is collected.

items.prompt: Put these steps in order: calculate closing balance; estimate period receipts and payments; carry the closing balance forward; start with opening balance.
items.answer: Start with opening balance; estimate period receipts and payments; calculate closing balance; carry the closing balance forward.
items.explanation: A forecast begins with available cash, applies the expected cash movements, then uses the resulting balance for the next period.

items.prompt: For each action, identify the main trade-off: (a) demand faster payment from customers; (b) negotiate longer payment terms with suppliers; (c) take out additional finance.
items.answer: (a) Customers may be dissatisfied or buy elsewhere. (b) Suppliers may restrict credit or relationships may worsen. (c) Finance creates future repayment or risk obligations.
items.explanation: Cash improvements are not costless: each changes relationships, future commitments or business risk.

items.prompt: A profitable wholesaler doubles sales to credit customers. Which is the best explanation for a possible cash shortage? A. Profit automatically becomes cash immediately. B. More inventory may be paid for and more receivables may build up before customer cash arrives. C. Borrowing is always recorded as sales revenue. D. Higher sales remove the need for a forecast.
items.explanation: Growth can require cash for inventory and can increase the amount owed by customers, creating a timing gap before receipts arrive.

items.prompt: A firm has opening cash of £14,500. It forecasts £46,000 of receipts and £53,500 of payments. Calculate its forecast closing cash balance.
items.explanation: Net cash flow is £46,000 minus £53,500, which is -£7,500. Adding this to £14,500 opening cash gives £7,000. This result still depends on the receipt and payment timing assumptions being accurate.
